prompt: Which three things together identify a CloudWatch metric?
hint: The name is a third of it.

choices.why: Period and statistic are chosen when reading, not part of the metric.

choices.text: Name, unit and the timestamp of each point
choices.why: Unit and timestamp belong to each data point, not to the metric's identity.
Region and account scope the metric, but name and dimensions still identify it.
Right. Change any one and it is another metric.

prompt: Orders were published with `Service=api,Stage=prod`. A dashboard queries `Orders` with only `Service=api`. What does it show on AWS?
hint: A metric with fewer dimensions is a different metric.

choices.why: That is what moto answered; CloudWatch does not add metrics up unless asked.
Right. Nobody published a metric with only that dimension, so the query names one that does not exist, and the graph is empty.

choices.text: An error naming the missing dimension
choices.why: No error: an empty answer is what makes this mistake easy to miss.

choices.text: Production's orders, the first stage published
choices.why: Order of publication plays no part in which metric a query names.

prompt: A question arrives about a five-minute spike that happened four months ago. What is the smallest period CloudWatch can still show?

choices.why: Right. Between 63 days and 15 months, only hourly points remain.
One-minute points are kept for 15 days.
Five-minute points are kept for 63 days.

choices.text: None: the data is gone after three months
choices.why: Hourly data is kept for 15 months.

prompt: Ninety-five requests take about 40 ms and five take 900 ms. Which statistic shows that one customer in twenty waits almost a second?

choices.why: 84 ms is the latency of no request at all.
The median is 40 ms; it hides the slow five.

choices.text: A high percentile, such as p99
choices.why: Right. p99 is 900 ms here, the slow tail made visible.
It says how many requests, not how slow any of them was.

prompt: Using the nearest-rank method on 100 sorted samples, which rank (position counted from 1) gives p95?
hint: p% of the samples at or below it.

prompt: A page makes 20 requests, each with a 1% chance of hitting the slow tail. What is the probability, in percent, that at least one is slow? Answer to the nearest whole percent.
hint: One minus the chance all twenty avoid it.

prompt: Match each metric to the statistic that answers the usual question about it.
Why is a customer's id never a dimension?
hint: Each distinct value makes a metric.

choices.why: Numbers are accepted; the cost is what makes it wrong.

choices.text: Dimensions are visible to every AWS customer
choices.why: Metrics are private to the account.

choices.text: Dimensions cannot be longer than eight characters
choices.why: No such limit exists; the problem is how many values, not how long.

choices.text: Each id becomes a billed metric, multiplying the others
choices.why: Right. Twenty thousand customers turned 240 metrics into 4.8 million.

prompt: At 0.30 USD per metric-month for the first 10,000, what do 240 custom metrics cost a month?
With the Embedded Metric Format, where does a customer's id written in the same log line end up?
hint: Only what the _aws block declares becomes a metric.

choices.text: As a dimension of the latency metric
choices.why: Only the dimensions listed in the _aws block are dimensions.

choices.text: A log field, searchable, never a metric
choices.why: Right. One line is the metric and the detail behind it.
The whole line is kept in the log group.

choices.text: In a separate metric per customer
choices.why: No metric is made from a field the block does not declare.

prompt: In the dashboard JSON, what does `"..."` at the start of a metric row mean?
hint: It saves writing the same metric twice.

choices.why: That would be a SEARCH expression; ... copies the previous row.

choices.text: Copy the row above, then change it
choices.why: Right. The p99 line is the latency metric again with another statistic.

choices.text: A placeholder to fill in later
choices.why: CloudWatch reads it, and the widget draws the line.
Dimensions are matched exactly; there is no wildcard here.

prompt: Put the four signals of a service dashboard in the order this lesson places them, first to last.
hint: What customers feel first comes first.
trap: Errors before traffic is the slip: a rate needs the traffic it is a share of.

prompt: What is the text widget at the top of the shop's dashboard for?
hint: Think of the person paged at three.

choices.text: To make the page look finished
choices.why: Decoration is not the point; the words are for someone in a hurry.
Thresholds live in the alarms; text there would drift from them.

choices.text: It is required for the dashboard to save
choices.why: A dashboard saves with metric widgets alone.

choices.text: Who owns it, where to look
choices.why: Right. The person paged at night needs exactly that.
